3.10.1.1 Replication of Sonbul and Schmitt’s findings for declarative knowledge

This experiment has replicated the findings of Sonbul and Schmitt’s (2013) second
experiment for the development of declarative knowledge of technical collocations.
Both Sonbul and Schmitt’s experiment and my experiment found, firstly, that
participants gained substantial declarative knowledge (as measured in the cued-recall
and form-recognition tests) through repeated exposure to the collocations in supportive
contexts in incidental learning conditions—both typographically enhanced and

decisions.reason: Because input row 2456 (doi_r = 10.26686/wgtn.17143838.v1) is removed in original as a proven redundant version-DOI duplicate of retained input row 2422 (doi_r = 10.26686/wgtn.17143838), its dependent outcome field is set to undeterminable/null per the review instructions. Substantively, across Chapter 3 (pp. 49-97), Chapter 4 (pp. 98-147, a separate extension to non-technical V+N and prep+N collocations), Chapter 5 (pp. 148-167), and Appendix A (p. 191), Toomer (2019) explicitly partitions Experiment 1 into (1) its conceptual replication of Sonbul and Schmitt's (2013) Experiment 2 for declarative knowledge of technical collocations (Section 3.10.1.1, pp. 89-90, replicating all four findings: substantial gains over control, superiority of bolding over unenhanced reading, two-week retention, and recognition exceeding recall, while replacing decontextualised learning with bolding+glossing) and (2) its extension for procedural knowledge (Section 3.10.1.2, p. 90, attributing reading-only priming in immediate and delayed LDTs to the extended dose of 9 exposures across 3 sessions over 2 days vs. the original's 3 exposures in 1 session, partly fulfilling Sonbul and Schmitt's p. 153 prediction and corroborating dissociation), supporting 'successful' on retained row 2422.

decisions.quote: The results of the immediate cued-recall and form-recognition post-tests corroborate Sonbul and Schmitt’s findings: multiple encounters with the collocations produced substantial declarative collocational knowledge, and more declarative knowledge was produced through exposure to typographically-enhanced collocations (with and without glosses) than to typographically-unenhanced collocations. Procedural knowledge was found, but, unexpectedly, only in the reading-only treatment.
decisions.reason: Experiment 1 corroborated Sonbul and Schmitt's (2013) declarative-knowledge findings on the cued-recall and form-recognition post-tests, but unlike the original study—which found no procedural priming in any condition—it found a significant priming effect in the reading-only condition.
